title: What solar panels do on a cloudy day
description: Panels do not switch off when clouds arrive — they fade. On a grey day a solar roof still makes power, just less of it, and knowing roughly how much less turns weather into something you can plan around.

body.heading: Less light, not no light
paragraphs: Solar panels convert light, not heat or direct sunshine alone. Clouds scatter sunlight but much of it still reaches the ground as diffuse light, and panels keep working on it — typically producing a fraction of their clear-day output rather than zero.
Thin cloud might cost a fifth of the power; heavy storm cloud can cost most of it. The panel's job is unchanged; the sky is simply turning the dimmer down.

body.heading: Why it matters for saving
paragraphs: Because cloudy output is reduced rather than absent, a household's yearly savings depend on the whole year's weather, not on counting perfect days. Overcast climates still run large, worthwhile solar fleets for exactly this reason.
If you track a home system, compare months, not days: one grey week is weather, while a season's trend is information about your roof, your usage and your bill.

takeaway: Clouds dim solar panels rather than stopping them: output falls to a fraction on grey days, so judge a solar roof by its year, never by one cloudy week.
